title: The History of Pork — The Meat That Split Religions and Redrew Borders
fullText: In the year 1492, in the plazas of Seville, Spanish inquisitors set up long wooden tables loaded with roasted pork, and ordered terrified families to eat in front of a crowd. This was not a meal. It was a test. Refuse to swallow a single bite, hesitate too long, or wipe your mouth the wrong way, and a neighbor might report you to the holy office as a secret Jew or a secret Muslim. someone only pretending to convert to Christianity. Thousands of so-called conversos and moriscoos were investigated on suspicion that grew out of nothing more than what they did or did not eat at dinner. Over the following century, an estimated 3,000 people were executed by the Spanish Inquisition and tens of thousands more were imprisoned, tortured, or driven into exile in part because of rumors about pork. Historians even coined a word for the pork eating rituals used to prove loyalty, maranismo, from a term that literally meant pig. Genuine devotion to Catholicism had a taste, and that taste was pork fat. But there is one detail from this whole grim chapter that rarely makes it into the textbooks. The single food dividing entire populations, the food used to sort the faithful from the condemned was not some rare imported spice or a costly delicacy. It was pork, a meat you can buy today for a few dollars a pound at any grocery store on Earth in the form of bacon, ham, or a sausage link tossed carelessly onto a breakfast plate. Think about that for a second. A farm animal decided who got to live in Spain and who did not. So, how did an ordinary domesticated pig become one of the sharpest religious dividing lines in human history? A food capable of starting riots, redrawing empires, and marking borders that still exist on a map today. This story does not start in Spain. It starts almost 9,000 years ago in two places on opposite sides of the world that had never heard of each other when small groups of humans looked at a dangerous tusked wild animal and decided against all good sense to bring it into camp. The wild boar that once roamed the forests of Anatolia and the river valleys of China was not a gentle creature. It was fast, aggressive, and armed with tusks capable of goring a grown man. Yet somewhere around 7,000 years before the common era, in what is now southeastern Turkey and independently in the Yellow and Yangze River valleys of China, human communities began the long patient process of domestication. They did not know the word genetics. They were doing it anyway. Generation after generation, they favored the boores that tolerated humans, that grew fatter, that reproduced faster in captivity. Archaeologists have found pig bones at sites like Kyonu in Turkey and Giu in China dating back roughly 8,000 to 9,000 years with skeletal changes, smaller tusks, shorter snouts that mark the shift from wild to domestic. This was one of the earliest and most successful acts of animal domestication in human history. And it happened almost simultaneously and completely independently on two different continents. Pigs offered something almost no other domesticated animal could match. They converted scraps, roots, and garbage into meat with astonishing efficiency. They reproduced quickly, often producing large litters twice a year. And they required no grazing land, no shepherd, no long migration. A single household with almost nothing could keep a pig alive on kitchen waste and produce a source of fat and protein unmatched by nearly any other animal available at the time. In an era when survival often meant getting through a lean winter, this was not a luxury. It was insurance against starvation. In China, the pig became something far bigger than food. It became civilization itself. The ancient Chinese character for home, Jia, is written with a pig beneath a roof, a symbol so old that scholars still debate exactly when it first appeared, but its meaning has never been in question. A household without a pig was in a very real linguistic sense not fully a household at all. By the time of the Han dynasty, pigs were the primary source of meat protein across Chinese agricultural society. Farmed in every province, integrated into ritual sacrifice, medicine, and cuisine so completely that pork became and remains today the default meaning of the word meat in Mandarin. Ask for meat in a Chinese market for the last 2,000 years, and unless you specify otherwise, you were almost certainly asking for pork. dictates. Rome built its own pork culture on a different but equally intense scale. Roman writers like Kato the Elder and later Ply the Elder wrote detailed instructions on pig husbandry and Roman soldiers marched on rations that frequently included salted and cured pork. The Romans were the first culture to industrialize pig farming at something resembling scale, driving herds of thousands of animals from the countryside into the capital along dedicated roads, feeding a city that at its peak held roughly 1 million people. Pork was not just eaten in Rome. It was legislated. Emperor Ourelion in the 3rd century of the common era made pork part of the regular free grain and food distributions to Roman citizens. A policy essentially treating cured pork as a form of public welfare. A meat that fed the poor of an empire. Not bad for an animal that started out as a dangerous tusked forest pest. Ancient Egypt tells a stranger, messier version of this same story. Pig bones appear at Egyptian sites dating back thousands of years, showing the animal was raised and eaten, particularly by the poor and by farming communities along the Nile. Yet the Greek historian Heroditus writing around 450 years before the common era recorded that Egyptian priests regarded the pig as an unclean animal linked to the god set and that anyone who so much as brushed against a pig would rush to the river to wash clothes and all. Whether this reflects genuine widespread Egyptian religious practice or simply one Greek traveler's secondhand impression remains debated among historians, but the pattern is worth noting. Centuries before Leviticus was compiled, at least one major civilization along the Nile had already begun treating this particular animal as something spiritually suspect, even while still eating it. The ambivalence, sacred nourishment to some, ritual contamination to others, was already baked into pork's reputation long before Judaism or Islam ever entered the picture. But here is where the story takes a turn nobody expected. While pigs were becoming central to civilizations across East Asia and the Mediterranean, an entirely different reaction to the same animal was forming in the deserts and river valleys of the ancient near east. and it would eventually split the world in two. The prohibition on pork in Judaism is ancient, codified explicitly in the book of Leviticus and the book of Deuteronomy, which lists the pig among the animals forbidden because although it has a cloven hoof, it does not chew its cud. Scholars have debated the origin of this taboo for centuries. Some point to practical hygiene, arguing that pigs raised in hot, aid climates without proper sanitation were more likely to transmit disease, particularly the parasite that causes tchinosis. Others argue that the explanation is symbolic and religious rather than medical, tied to the animals status as an unclean scavenger in a specific cultural and environmental context, or to a desire to distinguish Israelite identity from neighboring cultures that did eat pork freely, including the Egyptians, the Canaanites, and later the Philistines and the Greeks. The truth is that no single explanation has ever been proven and honest historians will tell you the debate remains unresolved. What is not in dispute is the effect. By the time of the second temple period, abstaining from pork had become one of the clearest, most visible markers of Jewish identity anywhere in the ancient world. And it stayed that way. Roughly 1,200 years after Leviticus was compiled, a new faith emerged out of the Arabian Peninsula that adopted a nearly identical prohibition. The Quran explicitly forbids the flesh of swine in multiple passages, grouping it with kerrion and blood as forbidden or haram. With the rapid 7th century expansion of Islam across the Middle East, North Africa, and eventually into Spain and the Balkans, an entire second major world religion carried the same pork taboo across three continents. Two of the largest religious traditions in human history arising centuries apart in different regions under different prophets, arrived at the same conclusion about the same farm animal. That is not a coincidence historians take lightly. And it set up one of the strangest and most consequential fault lines in world history. An animal that was sacred nourishment in China, a public subsidy in Rome, and an absolute prohibition across the Jewish and Islamic worlds all at the same time. Christianity notably did not inherit the ban. Early Christian theology, particularly through the writings of Paul in the New Testament, explicitly rejected Jewish dietary law as a requirement for the new faith, and pork remained fully permitted, even celebrated, across Christian Europe. This single theological decision made in the first century would end up mattering enormously more than anyone at the time could have guessed. As Christianity spread across Europe and eventually collided with the expanding Islamic world along the Mediterranean and centuries later in the Balkans, pork stopped being simply a meat. It became a marker planted directly on the map of who belonged to which civilization. And no, that is not an exaggeration invented for a video script. Medieval European writers and later Ottoman administrators both understood explicitly and in writing that a village raising pigs was announcing something about its religious identity. And a village that did not raise pigs was announcing something too. The clearest place to watch this play out is the Balkans. And here is the detail that makes the whole story so strange. The border lines you can still trace on a modern map of southeastern Europe. The lines separating historically Christian majority regions from historically Muslim majority regions correlate in striking ways with old patterns of pig husbandry. When the Ottoman Empire pushed into the Balkans beginning in the late 14th century following its decisive victory at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, it brought Islamic dietary law with it. But it did not attempt to force conversion or dietary compliance on every subject. Instead, the Ottoman administrative system, known as the millet system, allowed non-Muslim communities, mostly Christian and Jewish, to maintain their own religious courts, laws, and yes, their own diets in exchange for a special tax called the Jiza. Pig farming, effectively banned or heavily discouraged in Muslim majority towns and near mosques, persisted and even flourished in the surrounding Christian villages, particularly in regions like Serbia, where the pig became something close to a national economic identity. In the 18th and 19th centuries, Serbia's single largest export to the rest of Europe was remarkably live pigs and pork products. so central to the regional economy that the period is still referred to by some economic historians as the era of the pig economy. When Serbia eventually fought its way to independence from Ottoman rule across a series of uprisings beginning in 184, the humble pig had quite literally funded the musketss. This was not just about seasoning food. Pig husbandry became a form of political and economic resistance. A quiet, sustained declaration of Christian identity that funded the very rebellions that redrrew the Balkan map. Here is the detail that makes this strange. The leader of that first Serbian uprising in 18004, a man named George A Petravvic, better known to history by his nickname Karaj, meaning black George, was himself a pig trader before he became a revolutionary commander. He had spent years driving herds of hogs north to markets in Hapsburg territory, learning the trade routes, the border crossings, and the Ottoman customs posts that would later become critical military knowledge during the uprising itself. Whether every detail of his early biography as recorded by later Serbian historians is perfectly accurate remains debated given how quickly national mythology tends to grow around founding revolutionary figures, but the underlying economic reality is not in dispute. Pig exports were for decades the single most important source of hard currency flowing into Serbian territory. And the roots, contacts, and capital built through that trade fed directly into the infrastructure of rebellion. A dangerous tusked forest animal tamed 9,000 years earlier on the other side of the continent ended up bankrolling the birth of a modern nation state. And when the borders of the newly independent Balkan states were eventually drawn and redrawn across the 19th and 20th centuries, the demographic and religious lines those borders followed. Orthodox Christian populations here, Muslim populations there mapped with real and lasting consistency onto centuries of exactly this kind of small local economic and dietary divide. And you will not want to miss what comes next, because the pork story is about to turn from strange to genuinely dark. Meanwhile, back in Western Europe, medieval Christian societies developed their own tangled, often absurd relationship with the animal that neighboring faiths refused to touch. Pork was not just accepted in medieval Europe. It was for centuries the default meat of the poor. Pigs could forage in forests, eating acorns and beach nuts in a practice called panage, requiring almost no investment from a peasant family. And a single slaughtered pig, salted, smoked, and preserved, could feed a household through an entire winter. In a world without refrigeration, this was not a luxury. It was the difference between surviving to spring and starving before it arrived. Charlemagne's 9th century estate management document, the capitular deillis, includes detailed instructions on the management of royal pig herds, treating swine husbandry as a matter of state importance. [snorts] But precisely because Christian Europe embraced pork so completely, the animal became an easy and deliberate tool for marking and later persecuting religious minorities living within it. Jewish communities across medieval Europe and later Muslim communities living under Christian rule following the reconista of the Iberian Peninsula found themselves defined quite literally by what they refused to eat. Here is the uncomfortable reality that this part of the pork story forces you to sit with. For centuries in Christian Europe and particularly in Spain following the completion of the reconista in 1492 when the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella conquered the last Muslim stronghold of Granada, the simple act of publicly eating or not eating pork became a matter of life and death. Following the Alhhamra decree of 1492, which expelled Jews from Spain who refused to convert to Christianity, and a similar decree targeting Muslims a few years later, tens of thousands of Jewish and Muslim families converted, at least on paper, rather than lose their homes and livelihoods. But conversion did not end the suspicion. It simply relocated it. The Spanish Inquisition, formally established in 1478, developed an entire apparatus of surveillance built around detecting secret adherence to the old faiths, and food was one of its sharpest tools. Neighbors were encouraged and in some periods financially rewarded to report households that were not seen buying pork at market. Households whose chimneys did not show the telltale smoke of a curing ham. Households where children mysteriously never seemed to eat bacon. Public pork consumption became a performance of Christian loyalty. and the refusal to eat it for any reason, including simple personal taste or illness, could be entered into evidence at a trial that might end in torture, imprisonment, or death at the stake during a public ceremony called an auto defe. Some conversos, in a grim historical irony, began performing exaggerated public displays of pork consumption specifically to avoid suspicion. a practice detailed in surviving Inquisition records and trial transcripts. This was not a battle. It was a food-based surveillance state, and it lasted in various forms for more than three centuries, with the Spanish Inquisition not formally abolished until 1834. The dark chapter does not end in Spain. Centuries earlier and thousands of miles to the east, pork had already become a weapon of humiliation and forced assimilation in other contexts of religious conquest and conflict. From crusader treatment of Muslim populations in the Levant to later European colonial administrators using pork, sometimes literally as a tool of domination. During the Crusades beginning in 1096, Christian armies invading the Levant frequently used pork consumption or forced contact with pig fat as a deliberate act of desecration against captured mosques and conquered Muslim populations. A practice recorded by chronicers on both sides of the conflict. And in a chapter that connects pork directly to one of history's greatest atrocities, colonial administrators of European empires in the 19th and 20th centuries occasionally weaponized the animal against colonized Muslim populations specifically because they understood its religious weight, smearing pig fat or blood on mosque walls or in documented incidents forcing prisoners to handle pork products as a form of religious humiliation. This is the part that should make you angry. Not because pork itself carries any inherent malice, but because for centuries, powerful people understood exactly how much an ordinary farm animal meant to someone else's faith. And they used that understanding as a weapon rather than as a reason for basic respect. But the pork story is not only a story of persecution. Buried inside medieval Christian Europe's total comfort with the animal is one of the strangest, warmest little traditions in food history. And it deserves its own moment here because not every pork story ends in tragedy. In the English village of Great Dunmo, a custom began according to local tradition around the year 114. Though the earliest surviving written records date to the 1300s, any married couple who could kneel before the local church and swear in front of witnesses that they had not regretted their marriage or argued for a single day and night since their wedding would be awarded a flitch, a whole side of cured bacon. The Dunmo Flitch trials run as a mock court complete with a judge, a jury, and cross-examination of the hopeful couple became a genuine public spectacle, drawing crowds from across the region. Winning couples were carried through town on a decorated chair. The flitch of bacon held a loft ahead of them like a trophy. Whether every couple who ever claimed the prize was being entirely honest with the jury is understandably a matter modern historians treat with some skepticism. But the custom itself survives in a revived form in Great Dunmo to this day, held roughly every four years. Bacon in this one corner of the world became not a test of religious loyalty but a prize for marital devotion. The same animal, wildly different stakes. This is where the story takes a genuinely surprising turn. Because the very same animal that divided empires along religious lines was at almost the same moment in history quietly building an entirely different kind of empire, an industrial one 4,000 m away in the United States. By the early 19th century, the city of Cincinnati, Ohio, had become the single largest pork processing center in the entire world. So thoroughly dominated by the industry that the city earned the nickname Porkopoulos. Cincinnati's location on the Ohio River made it the perfect hub for receiving hogs raised across the Midwest and shipping salted barreled pork down river to feed the rapidly growing populations of the American South and eventually cities across the Atlantic. At its peak in the 1840s, Cincinnati was slaughtering and processing well over 100,000 hogs in a single season, using assembly line techniques of division and specialization that predate and likely influenced the automobile assembly lines Henry Ford would later make famous. Workers stood at fixed stations while carcasses moved past them. Each person responsible for one single repeated task. a system contemporary observers called the disassembly line. This is the part that does not get enough credit. Decades before Ford ever built a Model T, Cincinnati's pork industry had already figured out that breaking a complex process into small, repeated, specialized steps could turn slow, expensive craftsmanship into fast, cheap mass production. The center of American pork production shifted westward to Chicago by the 1860s and 70s, supercharged by the expansion of the railroad network and critically by the invention of practical mechanical refrigeration for rail cars in the 1870s, a development pioneered in large part by Gustavis Swift, who realized that shipping dressed refrigerated meat directly from Chicago to eastern cities was far cheaper than shipping live animals. that needed to be fed, watered, and cared for the entire journey, only to lose weight and value along the way. Chicago's Union Stockyards opened in 1865 grew into a sprawling complex processing millions of hogs and cattle annually, and by the early 20th century, Chicago's meatacking district had become one of the largest industrial complexes on the planet. But industrialization on this scale came with a brutal human and sanitary cost that stayed hidden from the American public until a novelist decided to expose it. In 196, Upton Sinclair published his novel, The Jungle, intended as an expose of the horrific labor conditions faced by immigrant meatacking workers, men and women who lost fingers, hands, and sometimes their lives in unguarded machinery, working shifts of 10 to 12 hours in freezing, bloodsicked conditions for wages that barely covered rent. Sinclair later wrote a now famous line reflecting on the book's reception. He aimed for the public's heart and by accident hid its stomach instead. American readers were far less outraged by the treatment of immigrant workers than they were horrified by the book's graphic descriptions of unsanitary meat processing, spoiled meat relabeled and resold, and contaminated product reaching dinner tables across the country. The public outcry was immediate and enormous, and within months, Congress passed both the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act of 196, creating the foundation of the modern American food safety regulatory system that still governs meat production today. A novel written to defend exploited workers ended up instead protecting the meat itself. An irony Sinclair spent the rest of his life somewhat bitter about. Gustavis Swift's refrigerated rail car deserves a closer look because it is a genuinely strange story of stubbornness paying off. When Swift first proposed shipping dressed chilled pork and beef directly from Chicago to the East Coast, existing railroads refused to build the specialized cars he needed. Worried the idea would undercut their existing lucrative business of shipping live animals long distances. Swift, undeterred, financed the construction of his own fleet of refrigerated cars and struck a deal with a smaller railroad. Willing to take the risk, the gamble worked. Shipping dressed meat instead of live animals eliminated the cost of feeding and watering hogs and cattle for days on cramped rail cars, eliminated the weight loss animals suffered in transit, and eliminated the risk of animals dying on route entirely. Within a decade, the practice had reshaped the entire American meat industry, and the railroads that once refused Swift's business were desperately trying to get into it. Here is the uncomfortable irony buried inside that success story. The same refrigerated rail technology that made meat cheaper and safer for consumers also concentrated an enormous amount of economic power into the hands of a small number of meatacking companies. A concentration so severe that by the early 20th century, federal antirust regulators were actively investigating what became known as the beef trust for price fixing and market manipulation, a case that eventually reached the United States Supreme Court in 195. Industrialization did not stop at the slaughterhouse door. Through the 20th century, pig breeding itself was industrialized with breeds selectively engineered for leaner meat, faster growth, and larger litters, moving pig farming away from small family operations and pasture-raised herds toward the large enclosed confinement operations that dominate commercial pork production today. This transformation delivered enormous gains in efficiency and affordability, driving down the real cost of pork dramatically over the course of the 20th century. But it also generated its own modern controversies over animal welfare, waste management, and the environmental footprint of concentrated animal feeding operations. Debates that remain very much alive today. Now fast forward to the present and the scale of the modern global pork industry is almost impossible to picture without hard numbers. So here they are. Global pork production today runs at roughly 120 million metric tons of meat annually, making pork the most widely consumed meat on Earth by total tonnage, ahead of both poultry and beef in most recent years. China alone accounts for roughly 45% of all pork produced and consumed worldwide. A scale so enormous that a single Chinese national strategic pork reserve exists specifically to stabilize prices during shortages. Treating pork with the same seriousness the United States treats its strategic petroleum reserve. Think about that for a second. An entire nation maintains an emergency stockpile of a specific meat because price swings in pork are considered a matter of genuine social and political stability. The European Union and the United States round out the next largest producers with the United States alone raising and processing well over 100 million hogs annually across states like Iowa, North Carolina, and Minnesota. And on the other side of the same global market sits the flip side of this story's oldest divide. The global halal and kosher meat industries. Businesses built entirely around certifying the absence of pork and pork derivatives from food products. Now estimated to represent a combined global market worth well over $1 trillion when the full halal food and lifestyle economy is counted. driven substantially by demand across Muslim majority nations in the Middle East, North Africa, and Southeast Asia, alongside kosher certification serving Jewish consumers worldwide. The same ancient prohibition that once got people burned at the stake in Seville now supports a colossal, entirely legal, entirely peaceful global commercial industry built on avoiding exactly the animal that another industry just as massive is built entirely around producing. Pork consumption per person also tells its own story about how unevenly this history landed on different parts of the world. The average person in the European Union eats somewhere around 75 pounds of pork per year, roughly the weight of a large dog consumed one plate at a time. In the United States, annual per capita pork consumption runs closer to 50 lbs, split across everything from breakfast bacon to holiday hams to the everpresent hot dog. In China, per capita pork consumption has in recent decades climbed to somewhere between 60 and 70 pounds annually across a population of well over 1 billion people. Meaning the sheer national volume dwarfs every other country on Earth combined. Meanwhile, across large parts of the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia, home to well over 1 and a half billion Muslims worldwide, and in Israel and Jewish communities globally, annual pork consumption sits by design at essentially zero. Picture that for a second. One single animal produced and consumed at a scale of well over 100 million tons a year on one side of the ledger and completely deliberately absent from the diet of roughly a quarter of the entire human species on the other. No other major meat on Earth carries that kind of stark religiously drawn line straight through the middle of global demand. The financial world eventually turned pork into something even stranger than a meat. It turned pork into a number you could bet on. In 1961, the Chicago Merkantile Exchange launched frozen pork belly futures contracts, allowing meat packers, restaurants, and pure speculators to trade on the future price of bacon months or years before a single pig was even slaughtered. For decades, pork belly futures became such a fixture of American finance that the phrase entered popular culture as shorthand for chaotic highstakes trading, showing up in films and television as the punchline for a wild financial gamble. The contract was eventually discontinued in 2011 after trading volume declined. But for 50 years, the exact price of the meat used to make your breakfast bacon was quoted daily on trading floors alongside gold, oil, and wheat. Money did not just buy bacon. For half a century, bacon itself became money's favorite bet. But pork is far more than just food. And this next part tends to catch people offguard. Pig physiology is remarkably close to human physiology. close enough that pig heart valves have been used in human heart valve replacement surgery for decades, saving hundreds of thousands of lives. And pig insulin was for much of the 20th century before the development of synthetic human insulin through genetic engineering in the 1970s and 80s the primary source of insulin used to treat diabetic patients worldwide. In recent years, researchers have gone even further. And in January of the year 2022, surgeons at the University of Maryland Medical Center transplanted a genetically modified pig heart into a living human patient for the first time in medical history. A procedure called xenotransplantation that scientists hope could eventually help solve the chronic global shortage of human organ donors. The patient in that first case survived roughly two months before passing away. But the procedure has since been repeated with improving outcomes, and researchers continue pursuing pig organs as a genuine future solution to organ transplant waiting lists that currently include over 100,000 people in the United States alone at any given time. An animal once treated as spiritually unclean by roughly half the human population may end up within our lifetimes quite literally keeping human hearts beating. The pork industry has also faced its own modern-day catastrophe, one with echoes of the historical famines and epidemics that shaped earlier food histories on this channel. Beginning in 2018, African swine fever, a highly contagious and almost universally fatal viral disease in pigs, tore through China's hog population, ultimately forcing the culling of an estimated 100 million or more pigs across the country within about a year, roughly a quarter to half of China's entire national herd, depending on the estimate. [music] The outbreak sent global pork prices spiking, disrupted supply chains worldwide, and forced China to dramatically increase pork imports, briefly reshaping global trade flows for a single meat product in a way not seen since the industrialization of the 19th century. It was a sharp modern reminder that even in an age of vaccines, biocurity, and global logistics, this same animal humans first tamed 9,000 years ago can still bring an entire national food system to its knees within months. So, here is the full ark laid out end to end. It was there almost 9,000 years ago when frightened, tusked wild boores were coaxed into human camps on two separate continents at nearly the same time. It was there beneath the roof in the ancient Chinese character for home. It was there in the free food distributions of Imperial Rome. It was there, forbidden in the sacred texts of two of history's largest religions, arising centuries and continents apart, yet landing on the exact same prohibition. It was there, quietly funding rebellions in the pig economy of 19th century Serbia. It was there, weaponized on the tables and in the trial records of the Spanish Inquisition. It was there on the disassembly lines of Porcopouloolis, laying the groundwork for modern mass production decades before Henry Ford ever built a car. It was there in the pages of a novel that accidentally reformed America's entire food safety system. And it is there right now in your refrigerator, in a strip of bacon, a breakfast sausage, a slice of ham, sitting quietly in your kitchen with absolutely no memory of the empires it helped build, the borders it helped draw, or the people it once got burned at the stake. Not bad for a farm animal nobody in Seville trusted enough to let eat in peace. If any part of this surprised you, the pig economy funding a rebellion, the pork heart now beating in a human chest, the accidental origin of American food safety law, let me know in the comments which detail caught you off guard because I genuinely want to hear it. And if you enjoyed this one, do me a favor and hit subscribe because we have a lot more of these hidden food histories coming. And I will see you in the next one. [clears throat]

Đây là phần không nhận được đủ tín dụng. Nhiều thập kỷ trước khi Ford chế tạo Model T, ngành công nghiệp thịt lợn của Cincinnati đã hình dung ra chỉ ra rằng việc chia một quy trình phức tạp thành các bước nhỏ, lặp đi lặp lại, chuyên biệt có thể diễn ra chậm, kỹ thuật thủ công đắt tiền thành sản xuất hàng loạt nhanh chóng và rẻ tiền. Nhưng công nghiệp hóa ở quy mô này đi kèm với cái giá phải trả về con người và vệ sinh một cách tàn khốc vẫn được giấu kín với công chúng Mỹ cho đến khi một tiểu thuyết gia quyết định vạch trần nó. Năm 196, Upton Sinclair xuất bản cuốn tiểu thuyết The Jungle của mình, nhằm mục đích vạch trần điều kiện lao động khủng khiếp mà những người công nhân nhập cư thịt phải đối mặt, những người đàn ông và phụ nữ đã mất ngón tay, bàn tay và đôi khi là cuộc sống của họ trong những cỗ máy không có người bảo vệ, làm việc theo ca từ 10 người đến 12 giờ trong điều kiện lạnh giá, đẫm máu với mức lương gần như không đủ trả tiền thuê nhà. Sinclair sau đó đã viết một dòng nổi tiếng hiện nay phản ánh về sự đón nhận cuốn sách. Anh ta nhắm đến trái tim của công chúng và vô tình giấu đi cái bụng của nó. Sự phản đối kịch liệt của công chúng ngay lập tức và rất lớn, và trong vòng vài tháng, Quốc hội đã thông qua cả Đạo luật Thanh tra Thịt và Đạo luật Thực phẩm và Dược phẩm Nguyên chất năm 196, tạo ra nền tảng của hệ thống quản lý an toàn thực phẩm hiện đại của Mỹ vẫn chi phối việc sản xuất thịt Hôm nay. Một cuốn tiểu thuyết viết để bảo vệ những người công nhân bị bóc lột cuối cùng lại bảo vệ chính miếng thịt. Một điều trớ trêu là Sinclair đã dành phần đời còn lại của mình có phần cay đắng.
